data.text/html:
Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) & Image Compression

An explorable companion to Luis Serrano's video. Every matrix is a rotation, a stretch, and another rotation. Drop the smallest stretches and you get compression.

data.text/markdown:
Roadmap (follows the video's order)
# Section You get to...
1 Transformations & the puzzle drag the columns of a 2×2 matrix and watch the coloured unit circle become an ellipse
2 ||(A = U\Sigma V^\dagger||) play the movie rotate → stretch → rotate bead by bead
3 Dimensionality reduction squash the small singular value to 0 and watch the ellipse become a line
4 Sums of rank-1 matrices add outer products ||(\sigma_i u_i v_i^\dagger||) one at a time
5 The heart paint a pixel image and decompose it into components
6 Image compression slide the rank ||(k||) on a picture; read error vs storage
Colour language (used everywhere): blue = first basis direction ||(e_1||) / first column, red = second direction ||(e_2||) / second column, orange = singular values & singular directions (the key quantity). Beads on circles are rainbow-coloured by angle so you can follow each point, not just the shape (the "harder puzzle"). In heatmaps: orange = positive, blue = negative. In images: dark = 1 (ink), light = 0, as in the video.

1 · Transformations: every matrix turns the circle into an ellipse

The video starts with a puzzle: turn a circle into a tilted ellipse using only rotations and horizontal / vertical scalings (stretches and compressions). Then the harder puzzle: do it so every coloured bead lands in the right spot. A 2×2 matrix is exactly such a point-to-point map. With the video's ||[A=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\4&5\end{bmatrix},\qquad \begin{bmatrix}p\\q\end{bmatrix}\mapsto\begin{bmatrix}3p+0q\\4p+5q\end{bmatrix},||]the blue point ||((1,0)||) goes to ||((3,4)||) (the first column), the red point ||((0,1)||) goes to ||((0,5)||) (the second column). The whole unit circle lands on an ellipse centred at the origin. Drag the blue and red handles on the right: they are the columns of ||(A||). The orange arrows are the ellipse's long and short half-axes, of lengths ||(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2||). The dashed orange arrows on the left show which input directions get sent there.

data.text/markdown:
2 · The main equation: ||(A = U\,\Sigma\,V^\dagger||)

Two special kinds of matrix from the video: ||[\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{rotation by }\theta} \qquad \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1&0\\0&\sigma_2\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{scale horizontally by }\sigma_1,\ \text{vertically by }\sigma_2}||]The moral of the video: any matrix is rotation → horizontal/vertical scaling → rotation: ||[A = U\,\Sigma\,V^\dagger .||]Read it right to left, because the vector is multiplied by the right-most matrix first: ||(V^\dagger||) rotates the circle so the right beads sit on the axes, ||(\Sigma||) stretches along the axes only, and ||(U||) rotates the result into place. (||(V^\dagger||) is the conjugate transpose; for real matrices it is just ||(V^T||).) The movie below uses the matrix you set in Section 1. Press ▶ play, or scrub the slider.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Dimensionality reduction: when an ellipse is almost a line

The video's next matrix is ||[B=\begin{bmatrix}1.8&1.2\\4.4&4.6\end{bmatrix}.||]It still turns the circle into an ellipse, but a very skinny one: the points almost lie on a line. In ||(\Sigma||) the horizontal stretch is big (||(\sigma_1\approx 6.71||)) and the vertical one is tiny (||(\sigma_2\approx 0.44||)). All of that skinniness lives in the small number. "Who are we kidding? 0.44 is really small, let's turn it into a zero." Use the slider to shrink ||(\sigma_2||) while keeping ||(U||) and ||(V^\dagger||) fixed, and watch the matrix ||(U\,\Sigma'\,V^\dagger||) change.

The matrix becomes \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\begin{bmatrix}1.5&amp;1.5\\\\4.5&amp;4.5\\end{bmatrix}||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: two \u003cstrong\u003eidentical columns\u003c/strong\u003e, rank 1, det 0. The ellipse is now a line (a \u003cem\u003edegenerate\u003c/em\u003e transformation).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNote how small the change was: the matrix moved by exactly 0.44, the value you deleted. A tiny change bought a much simpler matrix: 2 numbers (1.5, 4.5) plus \"both columns equal\" instead of 4 numbers.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eBigger picture: \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\sigma_2||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e measures how far \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(B||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e is from the nearest rank-1 matrix. That is the whole idea behind compression.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Rank-1 pieces: a matrix as a sum of outer products

Look at the video's 4×4 example. Every row is a multiple of ||((1,2,3,4)||): ||[\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3&4\\-1&-2&-3&-4\\2&4&6&8\\10&20&30&40\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\2\\10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3&4\end{bmatrix} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 16 \text{ numbers} \to 8.||]That is a rank-1 matrix (an outer product). For a 1000×1000 rank-1 matrix: ||(10^6 \to 2000||) numbers. A random matrix is not rank 1, but the SVD writes any matrix as a sum of rank-1 pieces, ordered from most to least important: ||[A = U\Sigma V^\dagger = \sigma_1\,u_1 v_1^\dagger + \sigma_2\,u_2 v_2^\dagger + \sigma_3\,u_3 v_3^\dagger + \sigma_4\,u_4 v_4^\dagger, \qquad \sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\sigma_3\ge\sigma_4 \ge 0.||]Keep only the first ||(k||) terms and you get ||(A_k||), the closest rank-||(k||) matrix to ||(A||) (the Eckart–Young theorem: it beats every other rank-||(k||) matrix).

data.text/html: Our 4×4 matrix ||(A = \begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 & 2 & 7 \\ 1 & 5 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & 8 & 12 \\ 7 & 9 & 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}||) has singular values 31.38, 4.96, 0.97, 0.16.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAt \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k=1||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e the first component already looks like a blurry copy of \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(A||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: same pattern of big and small entries. It is the best you can do with a single outer product.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eStep \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k = 2, 3, 4||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. Each new term is \"lighter\" (smaller \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\sigma||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e) and fixes less. At \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k=4||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e the error is 0, because a 4×4 matrix has at most rank 4.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe error norm equals \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\sqrt{\\sigma_{k+1}^2+\\dots}||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e, the dropped singular values. Small tail means a cheap approximation.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eStorage: here \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k(m+n+1)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e only beats 16 at \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k=1||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. The pay-off comes with big matrices such as images.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · The heart: an image is a matrix

The video's finale: write a pixel image as a matrix, 1 for black, 0 for white, and take its SVD. Each component ||(\sigma_i\,u_i v_i^\dagger||) is itself a little image, a rank-1 "plaid" (each row is a multiple of one pattern). Its strength is the singular value. Adding components from the left makes the heart sharper and sharper, and once the singular values hit 0 you can stop. The heart is exact. Paint your own image below (click/drag toggles pixels, presets on top). Then pick ||(k||).

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHeart\u003c/strong\u003e preset: component 1 is already a fuzzy heart. With a few components it is perfect, and every σ after the rank is (numerically) 0.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePaint a \u003cstrong\u003eSquare\u003c/strong\u003e or a \u003cstrong\u003eCross\u003c/strong\u003e: how many non-zero σ's do they need? A filled rectangle is one outer product, so rank 1. A cross needs 2.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe \u003cstrong\u003eDiagonal\u003c/strong\u003e looks simple but is \u003cem\u003efull-rank-ish\u003c/em\u003e: SVD can only build things out of horizontal × vertical plaids, so diagonal edges are expensive. \u003cstrong\u003eRandom\u003c/strong\u003e is the worst case: no structure to exploit.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Image compression: choose your sharpness, pay in storage

A real image is just a bigger matrix (||(m\times n||) grey values in ||([0,1]||)). Keep ||(k||) components: ||[A_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i\,u_i v_i^\dagger,\qquad \text{storage}=k\,(m+n+1)\ \text{numbers instead of}\ m\,n,\qquad \frac{\lVert A-A_k\rVert}{\lVert A\rVert}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2}{\sum_i\sigma_i^2}}.||]The image below is generated in the notebook (a little landscape, so no downloads are needed). "The sharper we want the image, the more storage we're going to need."

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='AjVT-0' random-id='08c723b4-dc00-ca05-e6f5-99957560b5ec'><marimo-slider data-initial-value='10' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003erank k\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-start='1' data-stop='150' data-step='1' data-steps='[]' data-debounce='false' data-disabled='false' data-orientation='"horizontal"' data-show-value='true' data-include-input='false' data-full-width='true'></marimo-slider></marimo-ui-element>

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eStart at \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k=1||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: horizontal × vertical bands only, a \"plaid\" sky. By \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k\\approx 10||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e the house and the mountains are recognisable at about 12% of the storage.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eFind the smallest \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e where you can't tell the difference (typically 25–40). Note the error there and the storage.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePush past the \u003cstrong\u003ebreak-even\u003c/strong\u003e \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: storing \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(U_k,\\Sigma_k,V_k||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e now costs \u003cem\u003emore\u003c/em\u003e than the raw pixels. Compression only pays when the tail of σ's is small.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe last error gains come from the 2% sensor noise we added. Noise has no structure, so it spreads over \u003cstrong\u003eall\u003c/strong\u003e singular values.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
7 · Sandbox: what makes an image compressible?

Pick an image, add noise, and choose ||(k||). The right panel shows the residual ||(A-A_k||) (grey = 0), which is exactly what you threw away. The log-scale chart shows how fast the singular values decay. A fast drop means cheap compression.

8 · Quiz: check yourself

Answer all, then flip reveal answers.

Recap

Idea Formula / picture Where you played with it

Every matrix = rotate → scale on the axes → rotate ||(A = U\Sigma V^\dagger||) (read right to left) §2 SVD movie

Image compression trades sharpness for storage ||(k(m+n+1)||) vs ||(mn||) §6 rank-k slider, §7 sandbox
Further from the video: PCA and matrix factorization (Netflix recommendations) are the same idea: keep the big singular directions.
